leading_positions.synthesis: Six of eight round-1 configurations prefer B007 (optical lattice clocks) as a single-part prize with Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. What is shared: the magic-wavelength idea as the enabling step, reproduction at about 1e-18 by several independent laboratories, and the concrete downstream uses (constants and dark-matter tests, relativistic geodesy, the pending redefinition of the second). Citation wording differs only in emphasis (invention and realisation, development, accuracy versus stability). Three of the six (Eriksson, Johansson, Pearce) moved to B007 after ranking something else first in the opening, so the support is partly a product of reading each other's ballots. Every supporter also lists the same reservations: overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, the unsettled priority of others (Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov, ion-clock groups), and the unfinished SI redefinition. Several rely on recollection for the 2001-2003 priority record.

One configuration prefers B012 (IceCube and high-energy astrophysical neutrinos) as a single-part prize, with Francis Halzen and Albrecht Karle only. The case is that this is a discovery of a clue from nature, supported by several independent analysis channels, and that it has become multimessenger astronomy (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane). The proposer himself calls support thin and names attribution as the main weakness: collaboration size, AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, and Yoshida's inclusion on the shortlist. B012 appears as an alternative in the files of Kroll and Olsson, and the chair's own file keeps it as an alternative, but alternatives are not counted here as preferences.

One configuration prefers B032 (fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics) with Christopher Jarzynski, Denis J. Evans and Udo Seifert. The case is exactness, generality and thirty years of experimental confirmation. The proposer concedes that the priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert cannot be resolved within three names, and lists B007 as her first alternative. No other member's preferred configuration includes B032, and no one has yet addressed its physics.

areas_of_agreement: All eight files, including the two that do not prefer B007, accept that the lattice-clock result is reproduced across independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL) and that the stated 1e-18 performance is established.

Every member who discusses B007 names the same three reservations as the strongest objections: overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, priority of others outside the credited pair, and the SI second not yet redefined.
All six B007 supporters propose exactly the same laureates (Katori and Ye) as a single-part prize, so there is no disagreement about the credited set among them.

Two members (Danielsson, Mehlig) who do not prefer B007 still list it as their first alternative, and Danielsson asks whether the committee should accept the clearest-attribution, broadest-support option (B007) over a stronger discovery case with narrower support (B012).
Several members state that they cannot judge some priority questions from memory and want outside expert checks before committing.
scientific_disputes: Whether the lattice clock is a distinct discovery or an evolutionary improvement of precision spectroscopy honoured in 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (ion control). Supporters say the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate enabling idea that gives the stability advantage of many atoms. Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson explicitly record the opposite reading as a legitimate view.

Whether a prize should reward a measurement and instrument (B007) or a discovery about nature (B012, per Danielsson and in the chair's reservations) or a framework of exact theorems tested by confirming experiments (B032, per Mehlig). Mehlig raises the same question from the other side: whether theorems confirmed by experiments count as a discovery in the prize's sense.

Whether the evidence for individual neutrino sources (NGC 1068 at about four sigma) is sufficient, or whether the committee should wait for KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD or IceCube-Gen2 confirmation. Only the proposer of B012 has argued this in round 1.

Eriksson keeps a pull toward condensed-matter candidates (B018 DMFT, B005 twisted bilayer graphene), noting the open pairing mechanism and sample dependence in B005 and Metzner's absence from the B018 credit. These points have not yet been answered by anyone else.
attribution_disputes: B007: the credited pair is Katori and Ye, but Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov and the ion-clock groups (Al+, Sr+, NIST) are named by several members as potentially omitted. Olsson also notes that the first-demonstration versus record-accuracy credit is claimed differently by Katori's and Ye's groups. Supporters argue Katori for the concept and early strontium realisation, Ye for accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics.

B012: the credited set on the shortlist is Karle, Halzen and Yoshida, but Danielsson proposes only Halzen and Karle and leans against Yoshida. AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal precedents and a collaboration of hundreds make any two or three names contestable.

B032: three-name limit versus at least seven claimants; Crooks, Cohen, Morriss and Searles are left out, and Seifert's credit for stochastic thermodynamics as a framework is different from credit for a particular theorem.
Lindroth and Kroll both mention that a possible second prize part would be constrained by the three-person limit (one extra name beside Katori and Ye), and no candidate for that part has been agreed.
maturity_disputes: B007: whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second (Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson list it as a legitimate view, and Pearce says it is not decisive and disagrees mildly with waiting) or to treat the demonstrated 1e-18 performance and independent comparisons as sufficient.
B012: Danielsson calls the discovery over a decade old and not premature, but the astronomy (source identification) is still at the roughly four-sigma level.
B044 (circuit QED): Johansson asks whether it comes too soon after the 2025 prize; this is not defended by any member as a preferred option.

B005 (twisted bilayer graphene): Eriksson raises the unsettled pairing mechanism and sample dependence; B005 is a first alternative for Eriksson and Olsson and a second alternative for Danielsson and Johansson and Mehlig.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson (director of WACQT; same circuit-QED community, long-standing Chalmers collaborations): states that he should not weigh B044 as an impartial member. He lists B044 as an alternative.

Kroll (executive management team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology with Johansson): would recuse or at least disclose if B044 became a serious option. He also notes a PhD advisor Svanberg and a year in John Hall's lab, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye.

Lindroth (close collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH): would need to weigh recusal on B003. She also notes that she knows the B043 and B041 literature but has no personal links to the credited names there.

Olsson (fellowship at the University of Tokyo, exchanges with Tokyo, Kyushu and Tohoku; Katori is associated with the University of Tokyo and RIKEN): no collaboration or co-authorship with any shortlisted candidate, but disclosed as an institutional connection relevant to B007.
Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig: no specific conflict stated for their preferred configurations; Eriksson notes that B018 and B005 are close to his own field.
questions_for_round2: B007 supporters: what exact wording in the citation distinguishes the magic-wavelength lattice clock from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and from ion clocks that reach comparable accuracy?

Can any member who works in atomic physics (Lindroth, Kroll, Olsson) check against the record the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstrations, and state whether Katori and Ye is a defensible two-name credit, or whether Lemonde, Derevianko or Pal'chikov would have to be considered?

Should the committee wait for the redefinition of the SI second before awarding B007, or is demonstrated and independently compared 1e-18 performance sufficient? Members should state a position and not only list it as a risk.

Danielsson: if B007 stays the majority position, is B012 to be pursued as a single-part prize, or only as a possible second part? If the latter, can the committee name a defensible two- or three-person credit for IceCube (Halzen, Karle, with or without Yoshida)?

Mehlig: given that the priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Searles, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert cannot be resolved within three names, does B032 remain a first preference, and what in its attribution could be settled by external expert reports?

Eriksson and others who raised condensed-matter candidates (B018, B005): do you wish to propose them as a second prize part, and if so with which three-name credit, given the Metzner question for B018 and the maturity question for B005?
Does the committee want a one-part or a multi-part prize this year? If multi-part, which candidate other than B007 has the most settled interpretation and a credit of at most two further names?
summary.chair_observation: Six of eight round-1 configurations prefer B007 with the same two laureates, one prefers B012 with two laureates and one prefers B032 with three. Support for B007 is broad, but three of the six reached it by changing their opening first choice, and all six list the same unresolved reservations (novelty against 2005 and 2012, priority outside the credited pair, timing of the SI redefinition). The two dissenting positions each carry a stated attribution problem. The main work for round 2 is to test the B007 reservations against the record and to decide whether any second prize part is worth pursuing; the chair takes no position beyond what is in the files.
